description.sr_latin: Kako Srbi pišu poruke — pozdravi, planovi, skraćenice i svakodnevna komunikacija.
description.en: How Serbians actually text — greetings, plans, abbreviations, and everyday casual chat.

phrases.context: The most common informal greeting AND farewell. Works for both hello and goodbye.
phrases.notes: From Italian 'ciao.' Used universally among friends. Can also be used when leaving.

phrases.context: Slightly more neutral than 'ćao' but still casual. Safe for most situations.
phrases.notes: Literally related to 'zdravlje' (health). A friendly, all-purpose greeting.

phrases.context: Super casual texting greeting. Fire it off to a friend instead of a full hello — you're not really asking for a location.
phrases.notes: You don't actually need to answer where you are. It's just 'what's up.' Very common in texts.

phrases.context: How guys greet each other — a casual hello to a male buddy, with the 'bro' tacked on.
phrases.notes: 'Brate' is vocative of 'brat' (brother). Not literal — it's like English 'bro' or 'dude.'

phrases.context: Casual conversation opener. Expect 'ništa posebno' (nothing special) as a response.
phrases.notes: Literally 'what is there?' The standard follow-up to a greeting.

phrases.context: More direct than 'šta ima.' Actually asking how someone is doing.
phrases.notes: Unlike in English, people might actually tell you how they're doing. Be ready.

phrases.en: What are you doing? / What are you up to?
phrases.context: Common text opener. Checking if someone is free or just making conversation.
phrases.notes: 'Raditi' = to do/work. This is the present tense — 'what are you doing right now.'

phrases.context: Checking availability before asking something or making plans.
phrases.notes: 'Zauzet' = busy/occupied (masculine). 'Zauzeta' for feminine.

phrases.context: THE Serbian hangout invitation. Coffee culture is sacred. This doesn't always literally mean coffee.
phrases.notes: 'Ajde' = come on / let's go. 'Kafa' (from Turkish) means domaća, Turkish-style coffee — and 'na kafu' is really an invitation to hang out. Bosnians say 'kahva'.

phrases.context: Casual sign-off when you'll catch each other again the same day.
phrases.notes: 'Vidimo se' = we see each other (reflexive). Very natural farewell.

phrases.context: Sorting out logistics for a meetup. Natural follow-up to making plans.
phrases.notes: 'Naći se' = to meet up / to find each other.

phrases.context: Getting the specific time for plans.
phrases.notes: 'Koliko' = how much/many. 'Sati' = hours/o'clock.

phrases.context: Confirming plans. Sealing the agreement.
phrases.notes: 'Dogovoreno' = agreed/arranged. From 'dogovoriti se' = to agree/arrange.

phrases.context: Very useful text. Serbs are famously relaxed about time, so expect to use this... and receive it.
phrases.notes: 'Kasniti' = to be late. 'Malo' = a little. The 'malo' is doing heavy lifting — it might be 20 minutes.

phrases.sr_latin: Ne mogu danas, jel može sutra?
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Не могу данас, јел може сутра?
phrases.en: I can't today, is tomorrow okay?
phrases.context: Rescheduling plans casually — you can't make today and float the next day instead.
phrases.notes: 'Jel' is short for 'da li je' (is it). Very common in casual speech.

phrases.context: Calling off plans you'd already made, while showing you feel bad about it.
phrases.notes: 'Moram' = I must. 'Otkazati' = to cancel.

phrases.context: Genuine concern. When someone seems off or went through something.
phrases.notes: 'Jesi li' = are you. 'Dobro' = good/well. The 'li' makes it a question.

phrases.context: When you sense something's up or someone messaged something vague.
phrases.notes: 'Dešavati se' = to happen/occur. Present tense — asking about right now.

phrases.context: Asking someone to let you know when they get there. Common caring gesture.
phrases.notes: 'Javiti se' = to get in touch / to message. 'Stignuti' = to arrive.

phrases.context: When a friend hasn't been in touch for a while. Half joking, half calling them out.
phrases.notes: 'Nestati' = to disappear. 'Nestao' = masculine past. 'Nestala' for feminine.

phrases.context: Response to 'gde si' or when arriving somewhere. Also used when answering a call/text.
phrases.notes: 'Evo' = here is. Extremely common in daily conversation.

phrases.context: The default answer to 'šta ima?' Even if something IS happening.
phrases.notes: Classic Serbian response. Even if you just won the lottery, you might still say this first.

phrases.sr_latin: Sad ne mogu, javim se posle.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Сад не могу, јавим се после.
phrases.en: Can't right now, I'll text you later.
phrases.context: Quick brush-off when you're busy. Common and not rude.
phrases.notes: 'Sad' = now. 'Javim se' = I'll get in touch. Note: no 'ću' — future tense often dropped in casual texting.

phrases.context: Letting someone know you've reached the destination.
phrases.notes: 'Stigao' = arrived (masculine). 'Stigla' for feminine.

phrases.context: Checking what your dev friend is working on. 'Kodirati' is commonly used in Serbian tech circles.
phrases.notes: 'Kodirati' = to code. Serbian tech vocabulary borrows heavily from English.

phrases.context: Asking if something works — code, a link, a plan. Very versatile.
phrases.notes: 'Raditi' = to work. 'Li' turns it into a question. Works for code AND life.

phrases.context: Developer pain in Serbian. 'Pući' literally means to burst/crack — used for anything breaking.
phrases.notes: 'Pući' = to burst/break. Serbians use this for everything: 'pukao mi telefon' (phone broke), 'pukao mi mozak' (my brain broke).

phrases.context: Describing buggy code. 'Bag' is the Serbianized version of 'bug.'
phrases.notes: 'Pun' = full. 'Bagova' = of bugs (genitive plural). Serbian devs mix English tech terms into Serbian grammar.

phrases.context: A small mix-up happens over text and you want to wave it off — no big deal.
phrases.notes: Texted 'nmvz' — the first letters of 'nema veze' (lit. 'no connection'). The Serbian shrug.

phrases.context: Mid-message, you want to walk back or clarify what you just said.
phrases.notes: Texted 'msm', short for 'mislim' (I think / I mean). Tacked on to soften or correct.

phrases.context: You want to tack a side note onto your message — the Serbian 'by the way'.
phrases.notes: Texted 'btj' for 'bilo to jest'. Honestly, most young Serbians just text the English 'btw'.

phrases.en: Oh well / It is what it is
phrases.context: Plans fall through and there's nothing to be done — text the resigned 'oh well'.
phrases.notes: Texted 'jbg', short for 'jebiga'. Technically a swear but as normalized as 'damn' — pure resigned acceptance.

phrases.context: The standard casual goodbye over text or phone. Literally 'we hear each other.'
phrases.notes: 'Čujemo se' = we hear each other. Used for phone/text sign-off. Very natural.

phrases.context: When you need to leave a conversation or a place. Direct but not rude.
phrases.notes: 'Moram' = I must. 'Da idem' = to go. Standard sign-off.

phrases.context: Casual sign-off promising to pick the conversation back up another time.
phrases.notes: 'Pričati se' = to talk (to each other). Very casual.

phrases.context: Casual goodnight to a friend. 'Brt' is the texting abbreviation of 'brate.'
phrases.notes: 'Brt' = short for 'brate' (brother/bro). You'll see this everywhere in Serbian texts.

phrases.context: Important question in Serbia, where food is central to socializing.
phrases.notes: 'Gladna' = hungry (feminine). 'Gladan' for masculine.

phrases.context: Suggesting food. In Serbia, this is always a good idea.
phrases.notes: 'Jesti' = to eat. 'Nešto' = something.

phrases.en: Where are we going out tonight?
phrases.context: Planning a night out. Serbian nightlife culture is strong.
phrases.notes: 'Izlaziti' = to go out. 'Večeras' = tonight.

phrases.context: The classic 'I'm bored' text that leads to spontaneous plans.
phrases.notes: 'Negde' = somewhere. Serbians are great at spontaneous plans.
